name: Log Cabin
lede: Log Cabin is a near-neutral dark grey-brown from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary, sitting in a crowded cluster of dark neutrals that includes Plum Grey and Greyish Black.

sections.title: A near-neutral from a dictionary, not Ridgway
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 *A Dictionary of Color* carries this tone on plate 55, A 5, first recorded there in 1923, and the 1955 ISCC-NBS circular cites the same entry, naming it brownish gray [1]. Its Munsell notation is given simply as N 3.4, the "N" meaning Maerz and Paul treated it as essentially hueless [1].

Unlike most names, it carries no Ridgway plate; it belongs to the dictionary-of-color lineage on its own [1]. It sits in a crowded cluster of near-identical dark neutrals: [[starling]], [[plum-grey]] and [[plum-grey]] are each about 3.4 to 3.7 units away, and [[greyish-black]] about 4.0 units off, all close enough to be mistaken for one another on screen [2]. The name itself, evoking weathered wood, is not explained in the sources consulted here, so its origin is undocumented [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive matches this tone in 283 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.19 percent, as photographed, more common than 66 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 2.7 percent of the 1,674 paintings from that decade, 3.1 times its museums' expected rate [3].

Inside a painting it most often sits in shadow, in 37 percent of its 153 clearly-ranked appearances, a rank computed within each canvas so varnish cannot fake it [3]. It is also most over-represented in French paintings, 2.1 times the expected rate, found in 46 of the archive's 3,443 [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and the match is a computed color reading, not a pigment identification [3].
